The search for professional meaning when AI can do your work. You do not have to work in tech to have a stake in this. Everybody is welcome, because this involves everybody who works.

## Why now

Mustafa Suleyman runs AI at Microsoft. This year he predicted that most desk work will be fully automated within 12 to 18 months. He named accounting, legal, marketing and project management. *[[1]](https://fortune.com/2026/02/13/when-will-ai-kill-white-collar-office-jobs-18-months-microsoft-mustafa-suleyman/)*

A survey of 16,400 office workers in 16 countries found the opposite of what many fear. The people who use AI most spend less time working alone. They spend more time learning. Their team relationships are stronger. *[[2]](https://www.gensler.com/press-releases/global-workplace-survey-2026)*

A machine can do what you are paid for. What happens to the meaning the work gave you? The Japanese word for what makes life worth living is ikigai. Some say AI takes it away. Some say AI finally sets it free.

![The popular ikigai diagram: four overlapping circles, what you love, what you are good at, what the world needs and what you can be paid for, with ikigai in the middle](https://gfjctyxqlwexxwsmkakq.supabase.co/storage/v1/object/public/event-banners/descriptions/ikigai-explainer-v1.jpg)

This is the popular picture of ikigai. The Japanese neuroscientist Ken Mogi says it is not Japanese in origin. He says it misrepresents ikigai. For him, ikigai can be as small as a morning walk with your dog. *[[3]](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=a_2RIydy_NQ)*

## Agenda

1. Introduction and a live demonstration of the *[Clarity Meeting Principle](https://claritypledge.com/meet)*.
2. Everybody takes a position on the *[six contested points](https://claritypledge.com/stake/ikigai1)*.
3. Conversations in groups of three, three rounds of 15 minutes. Everybody takes turns as speaker, listener and observer. Two people discuss a point they disagree on: six minutes to understand one, then they swap and spend six on the other. The observer then takes three minutes to say back what they heard.
4. Questions and answers.
5. Optional: join us for dinner at a nearby restaurant.

We welcome critical feedback. If you think the structure or the points are wrong, say so at the event.

## Prepare for the event

To prepare, read the stories of six well-known people with divergent opinions on how AI changes work and professional meaning:

- **Simon Sinek**, author: "It's the humanity that's going to suffer."
- **Garry Tan**, president of Y Combinator: "One person, no intermediaries, no permission."
- **Naval Ravikant**, investor: "I have found that the happier I get, the more I am going to do the things that I'm good at."
- **Alan Watts**, philosopher: "It's a great thing if you can learn what the Chinese call purposelessness."
- **Arthur Brooks**, Harvard professor who studies happiness: "If that's how I see me that's a real problem isn't it."
- **Brett Codes**, developer, handed his coding to AI: "what is my purpose?"

**[Read their stories and take your position on the six points](https://claritypledge.com/stake/ikigai1?tab=stories)**

## How Clarity Nights are different

In many groups, saying "I did not understand you" is thought to make you look stupid, or to sound offensive. So people do not reveal gaps in their understanding. That is a problem, because a gap you do not reveal cannot be bridged. Over time the gaps pile up. They turn into mistrust, broken relationships, and conversations everyone avoids. It is one reason people stay out of public discussion. We are changing that. At our events, revealing a gap in your understanding is rewarded, not punished.

This event is organized by the *[Communication Activism Community](https://claritypledge.com/groups/cm)*.
